description: Experience the vibrant flavors of authentic Chinese Hot and Sour Soup, a culinary masterpiece balancing fiery chili, tangy vinegar, and savory umami. This comforting bowl features tender tofu, earthy mushrooms, and crisp bamboo shoots, all swimming in a rich, aromatic broth that invigorates the senses. It is a beloved classic, perfect for a chilly evening or as a flavorful appetizer.

instructions.title: Prepare Ingredients
instructions.text: Rehydrate dried wood ear and shiitake mushrooms in warm water for 20-30 minutes, then squeeze dry and slice thinly. Julienne the pork tenderloin, firm tofu, and bamboo shoots. In a small bowl, whisk cornstarch with 3 tablespoons of water to create a slurry. Beat the eggs lightly in another small bowl.

instructions.title: Cook Pork and Broth
instructions.text: In a large pot or wok, heat a tablespoon of oil over medium-high heat. Add the julienned pork and stir-fry until it is no longer pink, about 2-3 minutes. Pour in the chicken or vegetable broth and bring it to a rolling boil.

instructions.title: Add Vegetables and Tofu
instructions.text: Once the broth is boiling, add the sliced wood ear mushrooms, shiitake mushrooms, bamboo shoots, and julienned tofu. Reduce the heat to medium-low and let it simmer for 5 minutes to allow the flavors to meld.

instructions.title: Season the Soup
instructions.text: Stir in the rice vinegar, dark soy sauce, light soy sauce, and white pepper. Taste and adjust seasonings as needed, adding more vinegar or white pepper for desired heat and tang. This is where the hot and sour balance is created.

instructions.title: Thicken the Soup
instructions.text: Give the cornstarch slurry a quick whisk to recombine, then slowly pour it into the simmering soup while continuously stirring. The soup will begin to thicken. Continue stirring for about 1 minute until the soup reaches your desired consistency. Add more slurry if a thicker soup is preferred.

instructions.title: Add Egg and Finish
instructions.text: Slowly drizzle the beaten eggs into the hot soup in a thin stream while gently stirring in a circular motion. This will create delicate egg ribbons. Turn off the heat. Stir in the sesame oil and chili oil. Ladle the hot soup into bowls and garnish with sliced green onions before serving immediately.

tips: For a truly authentic taste, do not skimp on the white pepper and good quality rice vinegar; they are key to the soup's distinctive 'hot' and 'sour' balance.
If you prefer a vegetarian version, omit the pork and use vegetable broth. You can add extra mushrooms or rehydrated dried lily flowers for more texture and flavor.
Hot and Sour Soup is best enjoyed fresh. If you have leftovers, store them in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2-3 days. Reheat gently on the stovetop.
article:
Hot and Sour Soup: A Culinary Journey into Flavor

Few dishes capture the vibrant essence of Chinese cuisine quite like Hot and Sour Soup. This iconic appetizer, celebrated for its complex interplay of piquant heat and tangy sourness, has graced countless tables worldwide, offering a comforting yet exhilarating start to any meal. From bustling street markets in Beijing to elegant dining rooms in New York, its unique flavor profile makes it an undeniable crowd-pleaser. Today, we're diving deep into the art of crafting the perfect Hot and Sour Soup recipe, exploring its origins, essential ingredients, step-by-step preparation, and expert tips to ensure your homemade version is nothing short of spectacular.

## What is Hot and Sour Soup?

At its heart, Hot and Sour Soup is a symphony of contrasting flavors and textures. Originating from Sichuan cuisine but widely adapted across various regional Chinese cooking styles, it’s characterized by a rich, savory broth thickened with cornstarch, brimming with slivered ingredients, and brought to life by a delicate balance of chili heat and vinegar tang. The "hot" typically comes from white pepper and, optionally, a touch of chili oil, while the "sour" is predominantly derived from rice vinegar, sometimes complemented by Chinese black vinegar for a deeper, more complex tartness.

Beyond its distinctive flavor, the soup is a textural delight. You'll often find tender shreds of pork, firm tofu, earthy dried shiitake mushrooms, crunchy wood ear fungus, and crisp bamboo shoots. Ribbons of egg swirl gracefully through the broth, adding a delicate finish. It's a dish that warms the soul, awakens the palate, and leaves a lingering, satisfying impression long after the last spoonful.

## Ingredients You Need

Gathering the right ingredients is the first crucial step in mastering your Hot and Sour Soup recipe. Here’s a comprehensive list for a batch serving 4-6 people:

*   **Protein:**
    *   4 oz pork shoulder or loin, thinly sliced into matchsticks
    *   4 oz firm or extra-firm tofu, drained and cut into matchsticks
*   **Aromatics & Vegetables:**
    *   6-8 dried shiitake mushrooms, rehydrated, stems removed, thinly sliced (reserve soaking liquid)
    *   1/4 cup dried wood ear mushrooms, rehydrated, thinly sliced
    *   1 (8 oz) can bamboo shoots, drained and thinly sliced into matchsticks
    *   2-3 cloves garlic, minced
    *   1-inch piece fresh ginger, grated or minced
*   **Broth & Flavor Base:**
    *   6 cups chicken or vegetable broth
    *   1/4 cup rice vinegar (or a mix of rice vinegar and Chinese black vinegar for depth)
    *   2-3 tbsp soy sauce (use tamari for gluten-free)
    *   1-2 tbsp sesame oil
    *   1-2 tsp white pepper (adjust to taste for heat)
    *   1/2 tsp sugar (balances flavors)
*   **Thickener & Garnish:**
    *   2 tbsp cornstarch mixed with 4 tbsp cold water (cornstarch slurry)
    *   2 large eggs, lightly beaten
    *   1-2 green onions, thinly sliced, for garnish
    *   Cilantro, chopped, for garnish (optional)
    *   Chili oil, for extra heat (optional)

## Step-by-Step Instructions

Follow these detailed instructions to bring your Hot and Sour Soup recipe to life:

1.  **Prepare Ingredients:** If using dried mushrooms, start by rehydrating them in warm water for at least 30 minutes, or until soft. Reserve the soaking liquid. While mushrooms rehydrate, thinly slice your pork, tofu, bamboo shoots, and any other vegetables. Mince garlic and ginger.
2.  **Sauté Aromatics:** Heat 1 tablespoon of cooking oil in a large pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the minced garlic and ginger, and sauté for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
3.  **Cook Pork:** Add the thinly sliced pork to the pot and stir-fry until it's just cooked through, about 2-3 minutes.
4.  **Add Broth & Mushrooms:** Pour in the chicken or vegetable broth. Add the sliced rehydrated shiitake mushrooms, wood ear mushrooms, and bamboo shoots. If you reserved the shiitake soaking liquid, strain it through a fine-mesh sieve and add it to the pot for extra umami flavor. Bring the soup to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 10-15 minutes to allow flavors to meld.
5.  **Season the Soup:** Stir in the soy sauce, white pepper, and sugar. Taste and adjust seasonings as needed. This is where the "hot" comes in, so don't be shy with the white pepper if you like a kick.
6.  **Thicken the Soup:** Give your cornstarch slurry a quick whisk to ensure it’s well combined. Slowly pour the slurry into the simmering soup in a thin stream, stirring constantly, until the soup thickens to your desired consistency. It should be noticeably thicker but still pourable.
7.  **Add Tofu & Eggs:** Gently add the tofu matchsticks to the soup. Immediately afterward, slowly drizzle the lightly beaten eggs into the hot, swirling soup while stirring gently with chopsticks or a fork. This creates those beautiful, delicate egg ribbons.
8.  **Finish with Vinegar & Sesame Oil:** Remove the pot from the heat. Stir in the rice vinegar and sesame oil. Taste one last time and adjust the sourness with more vinegar if desired, or add more soy sauce for saltiness.
9.  **Serve:** Ladle the Hot and Sour Soup into bowls. Garnish with sliced green onions and fresh cilantro, if using. A drizzle of chili oil can be added for an extra layer of heat.

## Pro Tips for the Best Results

Elevate your homemade Hot and Sour Soup recipe with these expert insights:

*   **Embrace Dried Mushrooms:** While fresh shiitake can work, dried shiitake mushrooms offer a much deeper, more concentrated umami flavor. Don't discard the soaking liquid; it's liquid gold for your broth!
*   **Vinegar Timing is Key:** Add the vinegar at the very end, after the soup has been removed from the heat. This preserves its bright, sharp tang. If added too early and boiled, the acidity can mellow out too much.
*   **Don't Skimp on White Pepper:** White pepper is crucial for the authentic "hot" element of the soup, providing a distinct, pungent warmth different from chili heat. Adjust generously to your preference.
*   **Perfect Egg Ribbons:** Ensure your soup is at a gentle simmer, not a rolling boil, when adding the egg. Drizzle the beaten egg slowly in a circular motion while gently stirring the soup. This creates fine, delicate strands.
*   **Cornstarch Slurry Savvy:** Always mix cornstarch with cold water before adding it to hot liquid to prevent lumps. Add it gradually, stirring constantly, until you reach your desired thickness. The soup will thicken further as it cools slightly.
*   **Taste and Adjust:** The beauty of this soup lies in its balance. Continuously taste and adjust the levels of sourness, saltiness, and heat until it perfectly suits your palate.

## Serving Suggestions

Hot and Sour Soup is a versatile dish, perfect as an appetizer or a light meal. Serve it piping hot, garnished with fresh green onions and cilantro. It pairs wonderfully with other classic Chinese dishes such as fried rice, lo mein, spring rolls, or dumplings. For those who love extra heat, a small dish of chili oil can be placed on the side for individual customization.

## Variations and Substitutions

This Hot and Sour Soup recipe is incredibly adaptable, allowing for numerous variations to suit dietary needs or personal preferences:

*   **Vegetarian/Vegan:** Replace pork with extra tofu, more mushrooms (oyster, enoki), or shredded carrots. Use vegetable broth instead of chicken broth. Ensure soy sauce is vegan-friendly (check for additives). This makes for an excellent vegan Hot and Sour Soup recipe.
*   **Different Proteins:** Chicken breast or thigh, shrimp, or even thinly sliced beef can be used in place of pork. Add shrimp towards the end of cooking as they cook quickly.
*   **Spice Level:** Adjust the amount of white pepper and chili oil to your desired heat. For a milder soup, reduce both. For a fiery kick, add more!
*   **Vinegar Choice:** While rice vinegar provides a clean tartness, incorporating Chinese black vinegar (Chinkiang vinegar) will add a deeper, more complex, and slightly malty sour note. A 50/50 blend is often preferred.
*   **Gluten-Free:** Simply use tamari instead of regular soy sauce to make this a gluten-free dish.
*   **Additional Vegetables:** Feel free to incorporate other thinly sliced vegetables like carrots, snow peas, or water chestnuts for added crunch and nutrition.

## Frequently Asked Questions

*   **Is Hot and Sour Soup healthy?** Generally, yes! It's low in calories, packed with lean protein (pork, tofu), and rich in vegetables and mushrooms. The primary concerns would be sodium content from broth and soy sauce, which can be managed by choosing low-sodium options.
*   **Can I make this Hot and Sour Soup recipe vegetarian or vegan?** Absolutely! As mentioned above, simply substitute pork with more tofu or mushrooms and use vegetable broth.
*   **How long does Hot and Sour Soup last in the fridge?** Leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3-4 days.
*   **Can I freeze Hot and Sour Soup?** Freezing is not recommended. The texture of the tofu and egg ribbons can become rubbery or unpleasant after thawing. It's best enjoyed fresh.
*   **What makes it "hot" and "sour"?** The "hot" primarily comes from white pepper and optionally chili oil, while the "sour" is derived from vinegar, most commonly rice vinegar.
*   **Why is my soup not thick enough?** This is usually due to not enough cornstarch or not cooking the soup long enough after adding the cornstarch slurry. If it's too thin, you can mix another small batch of slurry (1 tsp cornstarch with 2 tsp cold water) and slowly add it to the simmering soup until it reaches the desired consistency.

Mastering the Hot and Sour Soup recipe is a rewarding culinary endeavor. With its vibrant flavors and textural delights, it’s a dish that truly embodies the dynamic spirit of Chinese cooking. So, gather your ingredients, follow these steps, and prepare to impress your taste buds with a homemade classic that rivals any restaurant version. Enjoy the journey of creating this iconic soup!
